extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art and architectural criticism; architects and historians interested in Byzantine/Venetian ornament and proportion
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and evaluation of Byzantine (Venetian) architectural features — proportions, capitals, archivolts, ornament, materials, and symbolism — to judge authenticity, design quality, and aesthetic effect. Emphasizes subtle measurement, naturalistic detail, and the interplay of mass, line, light, and color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular and minute harmonies of proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: These singular and minute harmonies of proportion indicate not only that buildings are of one school, but that they remain in their original form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small differences in measurement (e.g., two inches on nearly three feet) are meaningful; compare dimensions across elements (arches, archivolts) to establish common authorship and authenticity. Ruskin treats such subtle coincidences as 'irrefragable proof' of an architect's intense perception of harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural features added purely for proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor arches/porticos introduced not for use but 'to consummate the proportions of the façade' and to exhibit exquisite arrangements of shaft and archivolt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize features whose primary purpose is compositional balance rather than function — e.g., small porticos at the flanks of a five-door façade; judge their success by how they complete the façade's proportions rather than by utilitarian criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central galleries/loggias and plan-light relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Palaces universally had central galleries or loggias opening into apartments on each wing, admitting an immense amount of light and producing slender, light, graceful proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plans for a central loggia/arcade and measure the relative light admitted: these spatial devices contribute to the characteristic elegance of Byzantine palaces and should be evident in original arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bold detached cylindrical shafts for main arcades
rubrics_metrics.description: Central arcades are generally sustained on bold detached cylindrical shafts with rich capitals, while wing arches use smaller shafts assisted by wall portions becoming pilasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the structural rhythm: prominence of detached shafts in main arcades versus engaged shafts/pilasters in wings is a sign of original Byzantine compositional logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two great orders of capitals: convex vs concave
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two great orders of capitals in the world: one convex in contour (richness/freedom of fancy), the other concave (severity/discipline). Both occur in Byzantine work, but the concave group is longest-lived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize capitals by convex or concave profile; expect different ornamentation tendencies (convex = imaginative/rich; concave = severe/longer-lived, extends into Gothic). Use profile comparison to date or locate types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitals modeled on flower-types (natural analogues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals may be best represented by considering them formed on types of flowers — one on the water-lily (convex family), the other on the convolvulus (concave).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use botanical analogues (water-lily, rose, convolvulus, trumpet-flower) to read and classify capital forms; this natural-point-of-reference aids memory and discrimination between the two families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of Corinthian-derived concave forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Concave family examples in Byzantine times are principally in large capitals founded on the Greek Corinthian, used chiefly for nave pillars of churches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect pure Corinthian forms in nave/transept shafts (e.g., Torcello, Murano, St. Mark's); their presence and treatment (sharp thistle-like leaves, curling extremities) are diagnostic of ecclesiastical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byzantine preference for bold convex 'bell' capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Byzantine favorite was the bold convex or cushion-shaped capital (the 'bell stone' formed by cutting and rounding a square block), used extensively with rich surface carving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the convex bell form and its abacus; judge richness by surface chiseling and variety of carved motives. The convex type often dominates secular and many Byzantine external applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional/modulated profiles combining concave and convex
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine capitals often modify concave profiles by making them bulge at the bottom into convex bell-shapes, producing transitional profiles (concave above, convex below or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for profile transitions (e.g., concave sweep that bends into a convex bell) as a characteristically Byzantine adaptation; these hybrid profiles are diagnostic of regional taste and period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life (naturalism and variety) in ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Life: capitals are often differently fancied, many with 'no two sides alike' — leaves more founded on realities, birds and plants varied in pose; designs show the mind of the workman among living herbage rather than Greek precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value naturalistic variation and individualized carving over strict symmetry or formulaic repetition. Assess vitality by degree of natural detail, asymmetry, and apparent spontaneity (e.g., grapes, differing pendent leaves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth (grand, unifying masses and curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Breadth: excessive breadth of the masses — outlines given by grand and simple curves that cast minute detail into a gigantic mould, producing unity of part and subjection to an enclosing form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge compositions by the sweep of primary curves and the dominance of broad masses over minutiae. Successful designs show generalization and broad contours that unify intricate detail (anticipating later Italian greatness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of capitals: braided/chequered interlinking to unify pierced stone
rubrics_metrics.description: Braided or woven ornament (interwoven fillets alternately sinking and rising) was carved to bind intermediate surfaces of pierced stone, giving unity and repose to otherwise scattered perforations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On pierced slabs/traceries, look for braided binding motifs that provide visual cohesion; evaluate the quality of the interweaving (depth, alternation, enclosure of floral motifs) as an essential decorative response to functional perforation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reticulated veils and net-like braid enclosing floral motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute traceries surround capitals; braided work often encloses on each side a flower (derived from the lily) — the 'lily capitals' with external networks producing exquisite series of curvatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how traceries and netting are used to frame central floral motifs; the interaction of inner flower form and outer network is crucial to the capital's contoural variety and viewing effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perforation as source of interior light-pattern ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute and star-like perforations in slabs allowed interior light and air, producing exquisite internal decorations of light; externally, ornament was applied to prevent a 'scattered and spotty' effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both functional (ventilation/light) and aesthetic consequences of perforation. A successful design will produce pleasing interior light patterns and an externally cohesive treatment (braiding/traceries) to unify the facade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and typology of small sculptural devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Private palaces used small sculptures (crosses, upright oblongs, circles) set above or between arches, often with a cross as invariable ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine facades for recurring small sculptural motifs and their positions (center of archivolt, above windows, between windows). Their regularity and typology (cross/oblong/circle) are characteristic of early Venetian practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconography and symbolic meaning of sculptural subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculptures often carry Christian symbolism: sun & moon flanking crosses, peacock as resurrection, vine as Christ or union with him, dove as the Comforter; groups of contending animals refer to powers of evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret sculptural subjects within Christian symbolic vocabulary; accurate reading of iconography deepens understanding of a building's religious temper and decorative program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate asymmetry and small-side variation to engage the eye
rubrics_metrics.description: Care is taken to secure variety — no two sides of Byzantine ornaments are in all respects the same; small alternations and irregularities keep the eye entertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value intentional asymmetry at the level of detail (different motifs on different sides, varying boss shapes, etc.) as a compositional device rather than as 'fault'—it enlivens viewing and prevents monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mosaic/gold grounds and reflective interplay with sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: Mosaic of glass with gold leaf in the hollows provided reflective grounds behind dark traceries; in shadow the gold shows bright behind dark ornament, or, when white marble is in sun, appears as snowy tracery on a golden ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the intended light effects: the combination of carved marble and mosaic/gold backing is integral. Consider how shadow and reflection were exploited for visual enchantment; absence/restoration of mosaic alters original perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material palette and color harmonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafts and facings used veined or variegated marble; capitals/sculptures often of pure white marble relieved upon veined grounds; palette included bands of russet and green, disks of serpentine and porphyry; leaves and edges sometimes gilded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate material contrasts and color chords (purple with green, white sculpture on colored field) as essential to the original aesthetic. Look for in-situ evidence or traces (bands, disks) to reconstruct original polychromy and contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about restorations and detection of original fabric
rubrics_metrics.description: Restorations in Venice are carried on with 'too violent hands' to suppose that delicate refinements would be noticed in demolition and imitated in heedless reproduction; minute correspondences are evidence of original form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat modern restorations skeptically when assessing subtle proportion and detail. Use surviving minute correspondences and measurements to argue for originality; beware that crude restorations erase the subtle harmonies Ruskin prizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The necessity of attentive looking ('watching')
rubrics_metrics.description: We only do not feel Byzantine buildings because we do not 'watch' them; the eye is influenced by what it cannot detect, and most by what it detects least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage sustained, careful observation and measurement; subtle curvature/variation requires laborious looking to perceive but strongly affects aesthetic response—train attention to small proportional shifts and contour changes.
